rv.q: Being a comedy sketch stretched out to feature length, An Act of God inevitably has its longueurs.
Hayes has an entitled-narcissist vibe that differentiates him from Parsons's naughty-choirboy act, and that gives the jokes a brisk, bitchy swing.

Hayes, who kept us in stitches as flighty pal Jack McFarland on NBC’s “Will & Grace,” may not be “infinity” years old, as the script -- based on a Twitter feed by former “Daily Show” honcho David Javerbaum -- allows. But he isn’t the young kid we remember from a TV sitcom, either.
Jim Parsons brings his trademark neurotic energy to the role of God in this irreverent comedy, though the material doesn't always live up to his committed performance.
Even at just 90 minutes, “An Act of God” (directed by the prolific Joe Mantello) is long-winded and full of unoriginal jabs at easy targets, but it is cute and occasionally witty.
Fans of Will and Grace may boost the box office here but the Booth rocks with laughter for a divine Hayes.
The humor is scattershot. The social satire is mild. The characterization of God as a curmudgeon whose mysterious ways are simply quixotic is scarcely profound.

cn.t: Critics find this irreverent comedy amusing but lightweight, with strong lead performances from Jim Parsons and Sean Hayes elevating David Javerbaum's scattershot material that doesn't fully capitalize on its clever premise.

vs.sum: The Booth Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and clear views from most seats, though legroom can be tight. The theater's elegant, European-inspired design adds to its charm, while sound quality is consistently praised. Facilities are average, with typical restroom and concession offerings.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Not completely wheelchair accessible. Infrared devices available.
